column2: The Lord's speech to Moses introduces the land-boundary command.
Canaan with its boundaries is the promised inheritance Israel is entering, retaining both land and limits.
The southwest side runs from Sin toward adjoining Edom and begins at the eastern Salt Sea; selected southwest is not silently made south.
The boundary passes the Ascent of Akrabin, Senna, southwest of Kadesh-barnea, the settlement of Arad and Azmon, preserving the selected sequence.
Azmon leads to the Wadi of Egypt and ends at the sea, retaining both the turn and endpoint.
The Great Sea defines the sea boundary, with the repeated boundary statement retained.
The northern measurement begins at the Great Sea and retains the selected repeated the mountain, the mountain rather than substituting Hor.
column3: The doubled mountain expression is difficult English but reflects the selected running text. Apparatus and syntactic review are needed before smoothing or supplying a proper name.

column2: The repeated mountain phrase continues toward Hamath and the boundaries of Sarada; the selected for them is retained.
column3: The doubled mountain and pronoun shift from yourselves to them remain unresolved pending specialist review.

column2: Dephrona leads to Hazar-enan, completing the northern boundary without normalizing the selected first place name.
The eastern boundary runs from Hazar-enan to Shepham, keeping the direction and both endpoints.
Shepham, Arbela, springs, Bela and the eastern ridge of Chennara all remain; the selected additional Bela is not dropped.
column3: The anatomical ridge wording and precise geographical identifications require specialist review; no map-based harmonization is attempted.

column2: The Jordan leads down to the Salt Sea, completing the surrounding boundaries.
The land is allotted to nine tribes and half Manasseh as prescribed; the half-tribe's name is explicit in the selected text.
Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh have already received their allotments, retaining the ancestral-house qualification.
The two and a half tribes' allotments are across Jordan opposite Jericho, from the south toward the east; both directional terms remain.
A new divine speech introduces those responsible for allotment.
Eleazar and Joshua son of Nun are named to obtain the inheritance for Israel, with their representative role retained.
One ruler from each tribe is to participate in allotting the land.
Judah's representative is Caleb son of Jephunneh, beginning the ten-person list.
Simeon's representative remains Salamiel son of Ammihud, preserving the selected personal name rather than substituting Shemuel.
Benjamin's representative remains Eldad son of Chislon, not a substituted familiar Elidad.
Dan's ruler remains Bakchir son of Egli, preserving both selected name forms.
Manasseh's ruler is Hanniel son of Ouphi, with the connection to Joseph retained.
Ephraim's ruler is Kemuel son of Sabatha, retaining the selected father's name.
Zebulun's ruler is Elizaphan son of Parnach, preserving both identity components.
Issachar's ruler is Paltiel son of Oza, retaining the selected father's form rather than Azzan.
Asher's ruler is Achior son of Shelomi, preserving selected Achior rather than substituting Ahihud.
Naphtali's ruler is Pedahel son of Benammihud, completing the ten western-allotment representatives.
These men are commanded by the Lord to distribute portions in Canaan, retaining the closing appointment summary.
The Lord addresses Moses on Moab's western side beside Jordan opposite Jericho, preserving the selected setting.
Israel must give Levites residential towns and surrounding outlying lands from its allotted possessions; both grants remain.
Towns are for residence, designated lands for livestock and all four-footed animals; the selected animal categories are retained.
The distance outward from the town wall is two thousand cubits in the selected Greek, not harmonized to a thousand.
All four measured sides remain two thousand cubits, with east, southwest, seaward and north preserved and the town in the midst.
Six refuge towns plus forty-two additional towns are granted to the Levites, preserving the distinction within the total.
Forty-eight towns and their outlying lands are the stated total, agreeing with six plus forty-two.
Contributions are proportional to the inheritance received, with many from the larger and fewer from the smaller holdings.
A separate divine speech introduces the refuge provisions.
Israel's crossing into Canaan frames the command that follows.
The towns shelter a killer who strikes a person unintentionally, retaining the intent qualification.
Refuge protects against the blood-avenging kinsman until judgment before the congregation; the emphatic no-death-before-hearing rule remains.
Six towns are reaffirmed as refuges, retaining the repeated count.
Three towns lie across Jordan and three in Canaan, preserving the regional distribution.
Israelites, sojourners and resident strangers all have access for unintentional killing; the named groups are not collapsed.
An iron-object fatal blow establishes the stated murderer case and emphatic death penalty.
A lethal hand-held stone and resulting death establish the next case, retaining the weapon's capacity to kill.
A lethal hand-held wooden object and resulting death establish the parallel case; the repeated penalty remains.
The blood-avenging kinsman himself kills the murderer upon encounter, preserving both the personal emphasis and repetition.
Hostility, pushing, ambush and a thrown object remain in the selected conjunction pattern leading to death.
A fatal hand blow in wrath is followed by the repeated death sentence and the kinsman's action upon encounter; no repeated penalty is removed.
Sudden pushing without hostility or an object thrown without ambush introduces the contrasting accidental case.
A lethal falling stone, lack of knowledge, absence of enmity and absence of harmful intent all remain.
column3: The compressed stone construction and the subject of knowing need further grammatical review; the inherited wording remains provisional.

column2: The congregation judges between the striker and blood-avenging kinsman according to these rulings, retaining adjudication before rescue.
The congregation rescues and restores the killer to refuge until the high priest's death; the priest's anointing with holy oil remains explicit.
Going outside the refuge city's boundaries creates the following exception; the actual boundary crossing remains decisive.
The kinsman who finds and kills the killer outside the refuge boundary is not liable, retaining all conditions.
Residence lasts until the high priest dies; only after that death may the killer return to his possession.
The ordinance of judgment applies across generations and all settlements, preserving both scope dimensions.
Execution requires witnesses, and a single witness cannot cause death by testimony; plural and singular evidence are distinguished.
No ransom is accepted for the guilty killer's life, and the emphatic death requirement remains.
No ransom permits return from the refuge arrangement before the high priest's death.
column3: The compressed infinitival sequence concerning flight and renewed residence merits further syntactic review; its temporal prohibition is preserved.

column2: The repeated murder-staining of land and atonement through the shedder's blood remain, preserving the selected violent imagery rather than merely saying pollution.
The land must not be defiled because the Lord dwells among Israel; the future dwelling and present self-identification remain distinct.
Gilead's ancestry through Machir, Manasseh and Joseph remains; the petition is made before Moses, Eleazar and the ancestral-house rulers.
The Lord commands Moses both to allot the land and to give Zelophehad's inheritance to his daughters; divine Lord and human lord remain distinct.
Marriage into another tribe transfers the daughters' allotment away from the petitioners' ancestral possession, with the repeated loss retained.
The release would leave the transferred inheritance with the receiving tribe, preserving the concern about continuing tribal loss.
Moses speaks by the Lord's instruction and says Thus speaks the tribe, without importing the familiar evaluation that the tribe speaks rightly.
The daughters may choose whom they please within their father's clan; preference and restriction both remain.
No inheritance passes between tribes because each Israelite must hold fast to the ancestral tribe's inheritance.
The next-of-kin inheritance language applies to every inheriting daughter and to each Israelite's paternal succession; both related uses remain.
The prohibition of intertribal transfer is repeated with individual attachment to one's inheritance, retaining the parallel emphasis.
The daughters perform the Lord's instruction to Moses, introducing the narrated compliance.
Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, Noah and Mahlah marry their cousins in the selected order, which differs from their earlier listing.
The marriages remain within Manasseh's clan among Joseph's descendants, so the inheritance remains in the paternal clan's tribe.
Commandments, ordinances and judgments close the book, given through Moses on Moab's western side by Jordan opposite Jericho.
